level.description: Orchestrate containers at scale — understand Pods, Deployments, Services, and Ingress to run production workloads on Kubernetes clusters.

lessons.title: Kubernetes Architecture & Core Concepts
lessons.content_md:
# Kubernetes Architecture & Core Concepts

Kubernetes (K8s) is the industry standard for container orchestration. It automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications.

## Why Kubernetes?

Docker runs containers on a single machine. But in production you need:
- **Multiple machines** for redundancy
- **Auto-scaling** for traffic spikes
- **Self-healing** when containers crash
- **Rolling updates** with zero downtime
- **Service discovery** so containers find each other

Kubernetes does all of this.

## Architecture

```
┌─── Control Plane ──────────────────────────┐
│  API Server   Scheduler   Controller Mgr   │
│  etcd (state store)                        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │              │              │
┌────────┴──┐  ┌────────┴──┐  ┌────────┴──┐
│  Node 1   │  │  Node 2   │  │  Node 3   │
│  kubelet  │  │  kubelet  │  │  kubelet  │
│  Pod Pod  │  │  Pod Pod  │  │  Pod Pod  │
└───────────┘  └───────────┘  └───────────┘
```

| Component | Role |
|-----------|------|
| API Server | Front door — all commands go through here |
| etcd | Key-value store holding all cluster state |
| Scheduler | Decides which node runs each Pod |
| Controller Manager | Ensures desired state matches actual state |
| kubelet | Agent on each node, runs Pods |
| kube-proxy | Network routing on each node |

## Core Resources

| Resource | What It Is | Analogy |
|----------|-----------|--------|
| **Pod** | Smallest deployable unit (1+ containers) | A single apartment |
| **Deployment** | Manages Pod replicas & updates | A building manager |
| **Service** | Stable network endpoint for Pods | A phone number |
| **Ingress** | HTTP routing from outside the cluster | A reception desk |
| **ConfigMap** | Configuration data | Sticky notes |
| **Secret** | Sensitive data (base64 encoded) | A safe |

## kubectl Essentials

```bash
# Cluster info
kubectl cluster-info
kubectl get nodes

# List resources
kubectl get pods
kubectl get deployments
kubectl get services

# Describe a resource
kubectl describe pod my-pod

# View logs
kubectl logs my-pod -f

# Execute into a Pod
kubectl exec -it my-pod -- /bin/bash

# Apply a YAML manifest
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml

# Delete a resource
kubectl delete -f deployment.yaml
```

lessons.title: Pods, Deployments & ReplicaSets
lessons.content_md:
# Pods, Deployments & ReplicaSets

## Pods

A Pod is the smallest unit in Kubernetes — a wrapper around one or more containers that share networking and storage.

```yaml
# pod.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: my-app
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginx:latest
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
      resources:
        requests:
          memory: "64Mi"
          cpu: "250m"
        limits:
          memory: "128Mi"
          cpu: "500m"
```

You rarely create Pods directly. Instead, use Deployments.

## Deployments

A Deployment manages a set of identical Pods, handling scaling, updates, and self-healing:

```yaml
# deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-app
spec:
  replicas: 3    # Run 3 identical Pods
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: my-app:2.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: db-secret
                  key: url
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods
# NAME                       READY   STATUS
# web-app-6d8f9b7c4-abc12   1/1     Running
# web-app-6d8f9b7c4-def34   1/1     Running
# web-app-6d8f9b7c4-ghi56   1/1     Running
```

## Self-Healing

If a Pod crashes, Kubernetes automatically restarts it:

```bash
# Kill a Pod
kubectl delete pod web-app-6d8f9b7c4-abc12

# K8s immediately creates a replacement
kubectl get pods  # Still 3 Pods running!
```

## Rolling Updates

Update your app with zero downtime:

```bash
# Update the image
kubectl set image deployment/web-app web=my-app:3.0

# Watch the rollout
kubectl rollout status deployment/web-app

# Rollback if something goes wrong
kubectl rollout undo deployment/web-app
```

## Scaling

```bash
# Manual scaling
kubectl scale deployment/web-app --replicas=10

# Auto-scaling based on CPU
kubectl autoscale deployment/web-app --min=3 --max=20 --cpu-percent=70
```

lessons.title: Services, Ingress & Networking
lessons.content_md:
# Services, Ingress & Networking

Pods are ephemeral — they get new IPs when they restart. Services provide stable networking.

## Service Types

| Type | Exposes | Use Case |
|------|---------|----------|
| ClusterIP | Internal only | Backend APIs, databases |
| NodePort | On each node's IP:port | Development, testing |
| LoadBalancer | Via cloud load balancer | Production web traffic |

### ClusterIP (Internal)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

Other Pods reach this via `http://api-service:80`.

### LoadBalancer (External)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

```bash
kubectl get svc web-service
# NAME          TYPE           EXTERNAL-IP      PORT(S)
# web-service   LoadBalancer   34.123.45.67     80:31234/TCP
```

## Ingress

Ingress routes HTTP traffic to different Services based on hostname or path:

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: app-ingress
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: api-service
                port:
                  number: 80
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: web-service
                port:
                  number: 80
```

## Complete Traffic Flow

```
User → DNS → Cloud Load Balancer → Ingress Controller
  → Ingress Rules → Service → Pod (container)
```

## ConfigMaps & Secrets

```yaml
# configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "info"
  MAX_CONNECTIONS: "100"

---
# secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: db-secret
type: Opaque
stringData:
  url: postgres://user:pass@db:5432/mydb
```

```yaml
# Use in Deployment
envFrom:
  - configMapRef:
      name: app-config
  - secretRef:
      name: db-secret
```

lessons.title: Hands-On: Deploy a Microservice to K8s
lessons.content_md:
# Hands-On: Deploy a Microservice to K8s

Deploy a complete application stack — web frontend, API backend, and database — to a local Kubernetes cluster using Minikube.

## Setup Minikube

```bash
# Install Minikube
brew install minikube

# Start a local cluster
minikube start --driver=docker --memory=4096

# Verify
kubectl get nodes
# NAME       STATUS   ROLES           AGE
# minikube   Ready    control-plane   30s
```

## Step 1: Database (PostgreSQL)

```yaml
# postgres.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: postgres-secret
stringData:
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: mysecretpassword
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: postgres
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: postgres
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:16
          ports:
            - containerPort: 5432
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: postgres-secret
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_DB
              value: myapp
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  selector:
    app: postgres
  ports:
    - port: 5432
```

## Step 2: API Backend

```yaml
# api.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: my-api:1.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8000
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              value: postgres://postgres:mysecretpassword@postgres:5432/myapp
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector:
    app: api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
```

## Step 3: Deploy Everything

```bash
kubectl apply -f postgres.yaml
kubectl apply -f api.yaml

# Watch Pods come up
kubectl get pods -w

# Check everything is healthy
kubectl get all
```

## Step 4: Access the Application

```bash
# Expose via Minikube
minikube service api --url
# http://192.168.49.2:31234

curl http://192.168.49.2:31234/health
# {"status": "healthy"}
```

## Step 5: Scale & Test Resilience

```bash
# Scale to 5 replicas
kubectl scale deployment/api --replicas=5

# Kill a Pod and watch it recover
kubectl delete pod api-xxxxx
kubectl get pods  # New Pod automatically created!
```

## Challenge

Add an Ingress resource that routes `/api/*` to the API service and `/` to a frontend service. Use the NGINX Ingress controller.
